title: Tutorial V.III: Free Tasks
text:
This is the final tutorial of the course. You’ll have the opportunity to work on a project of your choice, implementing it with the tools learned throughout this course and leveraging AI assistance. Choose one of the projects below based on your interests! In the last session, you will then briefly demo your project in order to pass the course. We only expect prototypes here and it is perfectly fine if things still have bugs or are not fully functional. We just expect you to spend two to three hours outside of class on your project in order to pass. Make it as good as you can!






TipDevelopment Environment



We recommend developing these projects in standalone .py files rather than notebooks. Use an AI-assisted editor like VS Code to help with implementation.








NoteAI Assistance



For each project, start by breaking down the requirements into smaller tasks. Use these as the basis for your AI prompts to generate initial code structure and implementations. Don’t try to build everything at once - iterate!

title: Tutorial V.III: Free Tasks

Create a side-scrolling platformer game where the player jumps between platforms, avoids obstacles, and collects items.
Features to implement:

Player character with left/right movement and jumping
Gravity and collision detection with platforms
Obstacles that end the game on contact
Collectible items that increase score
Score display and game over screen

Key library: pygame

Build a tool that extracts text from receipt images and organizes the data.

Use OCR to extract text from the image

Training LLMs

Imagine learning a language by reading millions of books
Learns patterns in how words and ideas connect via tokens
Interconnected nodes with weights representing patterns
During training, these weights are adjusted
Once trained, applying them takes much less resources








Using a trained model is called inference.

title: Tutorial V.I: Programming with AI
text:
Pattern Recognition

Not like a search engine!
When asked, it looks for relevant patterns it learned
Like having a huge library in its “memory” to draw from
It can find patterns between concepts and your question
Knows only limited text at once (context window)








Managing context windows is crucial!

title: Tutorial V.I: Programming with AI
text:
Probability based responses

After each written token, it predicts “what should come next?”
Like an advanced version of the word prediction on your phone
Chooses the most likely next token based on training
But can’t actually “think” or “understand” like humans

Python’s dictionaries can be a helpful tool for handling such tasks by allowing you to store and retrieve information using key-value pairs. title: Tutorial III.III: Package Management
text:
Welcome to this guided tutorial on understanding packages and package management in Python! We’ll explore this concept through the lens of library management - how libraries organize, maintain, and share their resources.
Think of Python as your local library’s main building. Just like a library has:

A main collection (Python’s standard library)
Different sections (third-party packages)
A catalog system (a package manager, in our case uv)
Multiple branches (virtual environments / project folders)



Let’s break this down:

Standard Library: Like the core collection every library branch has:

Python comes with essential tools built-in
Data structures (lists, dictionaries, etc.)
Mathematical functions (sin, cos, sqrt, etc.)
Random numbers (random, choice, etc.)

Third-Party Packages: Similar to specialized sections in a library:

Data analysis packages (pandas, numpy) → Research section
Visualization packages (matplotlib, seaborn) → Art books
Web frameworks (Django, Flask) → Technical manuals
Machine learning packages (scikit-learn) → Advanced studies section

Package Manager (uv): Works like the library’s catalog:

Installing packages → Ordering new books
Updating packages → Replacing with newer editions
Uninstalling packages → Removing outdated books
Dependencies → “You must read Book A before Book B”

Project Environments (managed automatically by uv): Like different library branches:

Each branch can have its own collection of books (packages)
Different editions of the same book (package versions)
Specialized sections for different purposes (project-specific dependencies)


The best part? Most Python packages are free to use, thanks to the open-source community!






We use uv in this course for Python version management, virtual environments, and packages. See the separate guide for more details: uv setup.

Exercise 2.2 - Compare the Strategies
Send all requests through a cache with 3 slots, once with lru_access() and once with random_access(). Store the hit rates (hits divided by the number of requests) in lru_rate and random_rate. Which strategy wins?

# YOUR CODE BELOW



Code
assert round(lru_rate, 3) == 0.719, "Check your LRU hit rate"

TipPython ships an LRU cache



The standard library already contains an LRU cache: functools.lru_cache. It remembers the results of a function, so repeated calls with the same input are answered from the cache instead of being computed again.



from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=3)  # keep the results of the 3 most recent inputs
def slow_square(n):
    print(f"Computing {n} * {n} ...")
    return n * n

slow_square(4)  # computed
slow_square(4)  # answered from the cache, no "Computing" message

Computing 4 * 4 ...


16

Virtual environments are like having different library branches. Each branch can have:

Its own collection of books (packages)
Different editions of the same book (package versions)
Specialized sections for different purposes (project-specific dependencies)

This separation ensures that:

Changes in one branch don’t affect others (project isolation)

The Secretary Problem: hire now or keep looking?

You are hiring a secretary and interview candidates one by one
After each interview: hire or continue searching
Once you reject a candidate, you cannot go back
How to maximize the chance of hiring the best candidate?


The name comes from the 1960s. The problem is about finding the best candidate, not about secretaries. It is also known as the marriage problem or the dowry problem.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The setup in three lines

We have n candidates and interview them one by one
After each one: hire or continue searching
We can only rank candidates relative to those we have already seen (ordinal ranking)


Question: Where in your life can you say “this one is better than that one”, but not “this one is worth 7 out of 10”?

Ordinal ranking: we can say which of two candidates is better, but we do not have a score or an absolute scale. This is what makes the problem hard, we never know how good the best candidate could be.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping

Question: Any idea how we could fail?

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: Look at the first 37%, then leap
text:
Look at the first 37%, then leap

Look at the first 37% of candidates without hiring anyone
Remember the best candidate so far
Leap: hire the next candidate who is better than that one
This finds the very best candidate in 37% of all cases


This is the mathematically optimal strategy. It means we still fail 63% of the time, but this is the best we can possibly do. The 37% holds for a large number of candidates; with only a few candidates, the chance is even higher.

section: Picking at random gets worse with every candidate
text:
Picking at random gets worse with every candidate
Chance of the best candidate if we pick one at random:

1 candidate: 100%, 2 candidates: 50%, 3 candidates: 33%
4 candidates: 25%, 5 candidates: 20%


Question: Do you see the pattern?


Pattern: 1/n. Look-and-leap never drops below 37%, however many candidates there are.

Random choice gets worse with every extra candidate, because each individual candidate is less likely to be the best. The look-and-leap strategy does not have this problem: its success chance never drops below 37%, however many candidates there are, and with few candidates it is even higher.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
Why 37%?

Look at the first share \(x\) of candidates, then leap
Chance of getting the best: about \(-x \ln x\)1
In words: look longer and your benchmark improves, but the best may already be gone
Largest at \(x = 1/e \approx 37\%\)2

Where does this come from? You win if the best candidate comes after your look phase and nobody before them beats your benchmark. That happens exactly when the best of all earlier candidates was in your look phase. Adding up these chances for every position, with many candidates, gives about \(-x \ln x\), where \(x\) is the share of candidates you only look at.To find the best look phase, we only need to know where \(-x \ln x\) reaches its maximum. Setting its derivative \(-\ln x - 1\) to zero gives \(x = 1/e \approx 37\%\), where \(e \approx 2.718\) is the base of the natural logarithm. For the full story, see Ferguson, T.S. (1989) ‘Who solved the secretary problem?’, Statistical Science, 4(3).

section: Let the computer try it out
text:
Let the computer try it out

Shuffle 100 candidates into a random order
Look at the first 37 and remember the best one
Hire the first candidate who beats that benchmark
Check: did we get the very best?

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The same idea in code

import random
random.seed(42)

def one_round(n=100, look=37):
    candidates = list(range(n))          # n - 1 is the best
    random.shuffle(candidates)
    benchmark = max(candidates[:look])   # best of the look phase
    for c in candidates[look:]:
        if c > benchmark:                # first one who beats it
            return c == n - 1            # did we hire the best?
    return False                         # nobody beat the benchmark

wins = sum(one_round() for _ in range(10_000))
print(f"Best candidate found in {wins / 10_000:.1%} of rounds")

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: If you can be rejected, leap earlier
text:
If you can be rejected, leap earlier
Question: In dating, the other person can also say no. When to leap?

50% chance of rejection: leap at 25%
Formula: \(q^{\frac{1}{1-q}}\), \(q\) = chance that your offer is accepted1
In words: the more often you hear “no”, the earlier you leap


Life lesson: higher risk of rejection means we should be less picky. With q = 0.5 the formula gives 0.5 to the power of 2, that is 25%. If offers are always accepted (q close to 1), the formula gives back the familiar 1/e.
Example from Brian Christian: searching from age 18 to 40, the 37% rule says get serious at 26.1. With many rejections, start at 23.5.

How it works: after the look phase, you ask everyone who beats all earlier candidates, and each says yes with chance \(q\). You get the best only if the best says yes and everyone you asked before said no. More rejections mean you use up more candidates after the look phase, so you have to start earlier. The stated formula is the best look phase, for example 25% when \(q = 50\%\). As in the basic problem, your chance of getting the best equals the look phase. With \(q\) close to 1, it gives back 37%.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: If you can go back, wait longer
text:
If you can go back, wait longer
Question: What if you could return to someone you passed on, but they might say no?

Going back works only half the time: look at 61%1, then leap
If nobody better comes, return to the best you passed
In words: a second chance makes it safe to look longer


Example from the book: an immediate offer is always accepted, a belated one only with 50%. The safety net of going back shifts the look phase from 37% to 61%.

Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: If you know the scale, use a threshold
text:
If you know the scale, use a threshold
Question: What if you know how good each option is, not just how it compares?

Example: you know test scores, or the price per square meter of a flat
No look phase needed: take the first option above a threshold
The threshold drops as fewer options remain
Chance of getting the very best rises to 58%1


This is the “full information” version. With absolute scores and a known distribution, you don’t need to learn a benchmark first. The threshold starts high and falls as you run out of options.

Gilbert, J.P. & Mosteller, F. (1966). Recognizing the maximum of a sequence. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 61(313), 35–73.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: Fixed time instead of a fixed number of options
text:
Fixed time instead of a fixed number of options
Example: one year to find a flat, viewings come as they come

Question: How should we adapt our strategy?



Same principle: look for the first 37% of the time1, then leap
The number of options is not fixed: the harder we search, the more options we see


This holds if options arrive evenly over time. We can also decide how intensively we search, for example by viewing more flats per week. Searching harder in the look phase improves the benchmark.


Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: The burglar: knowing when to quit
text:
The burglar: knowing when to quit
Example: each break-in succeeds with chance \(q\), one failure means losing everything

Question: When should the burglar retire?



Stop after about \(\frac{q}{1-q}\) successes
With \(q = 90\%\): retire after 9 break-ins1
Same logic for any streak that can end badly: a winning run in the casino, a project that keeps growing in risk


Ferguson, T.S. Optimal Stopping and Applications. Lecture notes, University of California, Los Angeles, https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tom/Stopping/. The rule assumes the same haul every time: stop once your total haul is worth more than what you would expect to gain from one more attempt.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: In practice, people stop too early
text:
In practice, people stop too early

In about a dozen experiments, people leap earlier than the 37% rule suggests1
Question: Why might that be?
Searching costs time and effort, and the rule ignores that
If looking is expensive, leaping earlier can be the right choice


Experiments by Seale and Rapoport (1997). The 37% rule assumes that looking is free. In real life, every viewing or interview costs time, so stopping a bit earlier is often rational, not a mistake.
Side note for drivers: an increase in occupancy from 90 to 95% doubles the search time for all drivers. Each variation changes the rule a little, but the structure stays: options come one at a time, and you cannot go back.

Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.

section: The Secretary Problem: hire now or keep looking?
text:
The Secretary Problem: hire now or keep looking?


You are hiring a secretary and interview candidates one by one
After each interview: hire or continue searching
Once you reject a candidate, you cannot go back
How to maximize the chance of hiring the best candidate?



Notes
The name comes from the 1960s. The problem is about finding the best candidate, not about secretaries. It is also known as the marriage problem or the dowry problem.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The setup in three lines

We have n candidates and interview them one by one
After each one: hire or continue searching
We can only rank candidates relative to those we have already seen (ordinal ranking)

Question: Where in your life can you say “this one is better than that one”, but not “this one is worth 7 out of 10”?

Notes
Ordinal ranking: we can say which of two candidates is better, but we do not have a score or an absolute scale. This is what makes the problem hard, we never know how good the best candidate could be.

Step 4: Open the terminal
Where: VS Code
Why: The terminal is where you type commands. You type a command, press Enter, and the computer answers with text. We only need a few commands, and you can copy them from this page.
Do: In the menu bar, click Terminal → New Terminal. A panel opens at the bottom of VS Code.

macOSWindows


The terminal shows a line ending with %. That’s where you type.


The terminal shows a line starting with PS and ending with >. PS means PowerShell, which is exactly what we need. If you don’t see PS, click the small arrow next to the + in the terminal panel and choose PowerShell.



Good to know:

Copy a command from this page, paste it into the terminal and press Enter.
Paste with Cmd + V (macOS) or Ctrl + V or a right-click (Windows).
Some commands take a few seconds. Wait until the line with % or > is back before typing the next one.

Check: You see a terminal at the bottom of VS Code, and its line mentions programming-course.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 5: Install uv
Where: the terminal in VS Code
Why: uv is a helper that installs Python for you and keeps each project clean. You only install it once.
Do: Copy the command for your system and press Enter.

macOSWindows


curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh


powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"



Now close VS Code completely and open it again. This is important: only then does the terminal know the new tool.
Check: After the restart, the top left of VS Code must show PROGRAMMING-COURSE again. If it doesn’t, click File → Open Recent → programming-course. Then open a new terminal with Terminal → New Terminal.
Check: Type this and press Enter:
uv --version
You should see something like uv 0.11.26. The exact number doesn’t matter.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 6: Install Python
Where: the terminal in VS Code
Why: This installs the Python language itself. Everyone in the course uses the same version, so the code works the same for all.
Do:
uv python install 3.13
Check: The terminal says that Python 3.13 was installed, or that it is already installed. Both are fine.

title: Installation Guide
section: Step 7: Turn your folder into a Python project
text:
Step 7: Turn your folder into a Python project
Where: the terminal in VS Code, inside programming-course
Why: This tells uv: “this folder is a Python project”. uv creates a few files it needs to keep track of things.
Check first: The terminal must be inside your course folder. Type this and press Enter:

macOSWindows


pwd


Get-Location



The answer must end with programming-course. If it doesn’t: close the terminal (the bin icon in the terminal panel), open the folder with File → Open Recent → programming-course, and open a new terminal with Terminal → New Terminal.
Do: Run this command:
uv init --python 3.13
The --python 3.13 part tells uv that this project uses Python 3.13, and that 3.13 is the minimum version it needs.
New files appear on the left in VS Code. You don’t need to touch them:

main.py: a tiny example program
pyproject.toml: the list of what your project needs
.python-version: which Python version the project uses

Check: Run the example program:
uv run python main.py
You should see Hello from programming-course!. Congratulations, you just ran your first Python program!

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 8: Add notebook support
Where: the terminal in VS Code
Why: Notebooks need two extra helpers. The first one lets notebooks use the Python of your project, the second one adds the notebook tools.
Do:
uv add --dev ipykernel
uv add jupyter
Check: The terminal lists a lot of installed packages and ends without an error. A new folder .venv appears on the left. That’s your project’s own Python environment.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 9: Your first notebook
Where: VS Code
Why: This checks that everything works together, before you start with the tutorials.
Do:

Press Cmd + Shift + P (macOS) or Ctrl + Shift + P (Windows). A search bar opens at the top.
Type Create: New Jupyter Notebook and press Enter.
Click Select Kernel in the top right corner. The kernel is the Python that runs your notebook.
Choose Python Environments, then the one that says .venv and Python 3.13.
Click into the first cell, type print("Hello") and press Shift + Enter.

Check: Below the cell, you see Hello. Everything works!
If VS Code asks to install extensions at any point, click Install.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 10: Open a tutorial
Where: your web browser, then VS Code
Do:

Open a tutorial on the course website.
On the right side under Other Formats, click Jupyter to download the notebook.
Move the downloaded file into your programming-course folder.
Open it in VS Code by clicking it on the left.
If VS Code asks for a kernel, choose the same .venv with Python 3.13 as in Step 9.

You’re ready for the tutorials!

title: Installation Guide
text:
Checklist

VS Code is installed and opens
The Python and Jupyter extensions are installed
You have a folder programming-course and opened it in VS Code
uv --version shows a version number
uv run python main.py shows Hello from programming-course!
A notebook cell with print("Hello") shows Hello

text:
Every next session
You don’t need to install anything again. Just:

Open VS Code.
Click File → Open Recent → programming-course.
Open the notebook you want to work on.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Something doesn’t work?







Problem
What to do




uv is “not found” or “not recognized”
Close VS Code completely and open it again. On Windows, check that the terminal says PS.


main.py can’t be found
Check the folder and the terminal as in Step 7, then run uv init --python 3.13 again in the right folder. If uv init ran in a different folder by mistake: don’t delete anything, ask us.


uv says the Python version is incompatible with the project
Open pyproject.toml in VS Code and change the line requires-python to requires-python = ">=3.13". Save the file, then run uv python pin 3.13 and uv sync.


Windows says scripts are disabled
Run Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope Process, then repeat Step 5.


.venv doesn’t appear under Select Kernel
Press Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + P, type Developer: Reload Window, press Enter, try again.


The notebook shows a different Python than 3.13
Click on the kernel name in the top right and choose the .venv one.


uv self update fails on a Mac
If you installed uv with Homebrew, use brew upgrade uv instead.


Anything else
Ask us! Guessing usually takes longer than asking.

Complex Conditions

Nested if Statements: Use if statements inside other if statements.
Logical Operators: Combine conditions using and, or, not.
Structure:

if (condition1) and (condition2):
    # code if both conditions are True
elif (condition1) or (condition2):
    # code if at least one condition is True

    # code if none of the conditions are True

Lists

Definition: Ordered, mutable collections of items.
Creation: Use square brackets [].


ratings = [4.5, 3.8, 4.2]

Indexing: Use [index] to access elements.


print(restaurants[0])  # Access the first element

Magic Place



Negative Indexing: Use [-1] to access the last element.


print(restaurants[-1])  # Access the last element

Coffee Shop



Slicing: Use [start:end] to access a range of elements.


print(restaurants[0:2])  # Access the first two elements

Appending: Use append() to add an element to the end of the list.


restaurants.append("Pasta Place")


Inserting: Use insert() to add an element at a specific index.


restaurants.insert(0, "Pasta Magic")

]

Tuples

Definition: Ordered, immutable collections of items.
Creation: Use parentheses ().
Immutability: Once created, cannot be changed.
Memory Efficiency: Use less memory than lists.
Use Cases: Ideal for fixed data (e.g., restaurant location).


ratings = (4.5, 3.8, 4.2)

break and continue

break: Exit the loop.
continue: Skip the current iteration and continue with the next.


efficacy_scores = [45, 60, 75, 85, 90]
for score in efficacy_scores:

    if score >= 85:

Definition: Assign elements of a tuple to variables.
Structure: a, b, c = some_tuple (as many variables as elements)

while Loops

Definition: Execute code repeatedly as long as a condition is true.
Structure:

while condition:
    # code to execute while condition is True

text:
Basic Function

Definition: Use the def keyword.
Structure:

def function_name(parameters):
    # code to execute (function body)
    return value  # Optional

Example:


def greet_visitor(name):
    return f"Welcome to the library, {name}!"

greet_visitor("Student")

'Welcome to the library, Student!'

title: Cheatsheet
text:
Return Value

Definition: The value returned by a function.
Example:


def multiply_by_two(number):
    return number * 2

result = multiply_by_two(5)
print(result)

10



Note: If a function does not return a value, it implicitly returns None.

text:
Default Parameters

Definition: Provide default values for function parameters.
Structure:

def greet_visitor(name="People"):
    return f"Welcome to the library, {name}!"

print(greet_visitor()) # Calls the function with the default parameter
print(greet_visitor("Nils")) # Calls the function with a custom parameter

title: Cheatsheet
text:
Multiple Parameters

Definition: Functions can have multiple parameters.
Structure:

def greet_visitor(name, age):
    return f"Welcome to the library, {name}! You are {age} years old."

print(greet_visitor("Nils", 30))

title: Programming: Everyday Decision-Making Algorithms
text:
Course Description
This course explores the intersection of computer science and everyday life by examining how algorithms can be applied to improve decision-making in various contexts. Inspired by the book “Algorithms to Live By” by Brian Christian and Tom Griffiths, the course will cover optimal stopping, explore and exploit, caching, scheduling, randomness and computational kindness, with an outlook on topics such as game theory, providing both theoretical foundations and practical programming exercises. The course consists of lectures and exercises.

title: Programming: Everyday Decision-Making Algorithms
text:
Learning Outcomes
Our broad goal is to equip students with the ability to get to grips with algorithmic thinking. We want to enable students to independently apply methods and concepts from algorithms to solve their everyday practical problems while also providing a brief introduction into programming with Python.
Upon completion of the course, students will:

understand fundamental algorithms and their applications to everyday problems
develop the ability to model real-world scenarios using algorithmic thinking
implement simple algorithms in Python to solve practical problems
analyze the efficiency and effectiveness of different algorithms in various contexts

Please note that this course is specifically designed for business students. That is, it is not required to have any advanced knowledge or experience in programming to attend this course. The teaching format will make it possible to account for different levels of programming skills such that every student can take the most out of the course.

title: Programming: Everyday Decision-Making Algorithms
text:
Course Structure
The course is based on a hands-on approach with a two-fold structure:

Lectures: In the lectures, we will introduce and discuss concepts and illustrate them in reproducible examples.
Hands-on Tutorials: Students will apply the concepts from the lecture in Jupyter notebooks, while simultaneously learning the basics of Python.

The course is not graded and can only be passed/failed. To pass, you need:

Attendance: at least 75% of the lectures.
Assignments: two assignments, each on an algorithmic problem from the course. At least 50% of the solutions must be correct.
Presentation: a short final presentation of an implemented prototype in the last lecture, followed by a discussion in class.

All assignments are due by the end of the quarter, but earlier submissions are highly encouraged. You can work in groups of up to three students.
You can find more information on the course contents in the syllabus.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Explore gathers information, exploit uses it
text:
Explore gathers information, exploit uses it



🔍 Explore


Definition: Gathering new information
Risk: Unknown outcomes
Example: Trying that new sushi place





🎯 Exploit


Definition: Using known information
Risk: Missing better options
Example: Your go-to pizza joint












In any given moment you can only do one of the two.





Notes
The fundamental trade-off: explore and exploit are mutually exclusive choices in any given moment. You can’t have your cake and eat it too. Exploring means gathering new information with unknown outcomes, for example trying that new sushi place. Exploiting means using known information, with the risk of missing better options, for example your go-to pizza joint.

text:
A fair estimate: Laplace’s rule of succession


First we need a fair estimate of each machine
Laplace (18th century): after \(w\) wins and \(l\) losses, the chance of a win is about


\[\mathbb{E}[\text{win}] = \frac{w + 1}{w + l + 2}\]

In words: add one imagined win and one imagined loss, then take the share of wins


Notes
Pierre-Simon Laplace suggested this rule in the 18th century. The two added pulls keep the estimate away from 0 and 1 when we have seen very few pulls. The rule estimates how good a machine is; it does not tell us when to stop exploring.

section: Bellman: calculate backwards from the last pull
text:
Bellman: calculate backwards from the last pull


Richard Bellman found the exact solution for a known interval
Start at the final pull: with no future left, simply exploit
Then calculate backwards the best choice in every earlier situation



Notes
A few years after win-stay lose-shift, Richard Bellman found an exact solution for all cases with finite and known intervals. The question is when to stop exploring and start exploiting. The solution uses dynamic programming: start at the final pull and calculate backwards what the best choice is in every possible situation. This works because the last pull is easy.

Bellman needs to know how long you stay


The calculation grows fast with many arms and a long interval
Worse: we usually don’t know how long we stay in the casino
So the bandit problem seemed to have no practical solution

The calculation of the optimal strategy is very extensive when there are many arms and a long interval. And the approach does not help in many scenarios, because we do not know the exact length of the interval. At this point it looked like the multi-armed bandit problem would remain a problem without a solution.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Gittins Index: The Scary Math
\[G_i(s_i, f_i) := \sup_{\tau \geq 1} \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \beta^t \cdot r_i^t \middle| s_i, f_i\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \beta^t\right]}\]
In words: the best average reward you can expect from this arm if you may stop playing it whenever you like.







Too complex to calculate by hand, and you don’t need to: just use the lookup table!

Higher index, better choice


Core idea: “What’s the best possible average reward from this option?”
Higher index = better choice
Less-tested options get an exploration bonus, that’s why machine B wins
The index balances exploration and exploitation automatically

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Which rule when?


Both outcomes known: choose the higher expected value
E(explore) unknown, interval known: Bellman (backward calculation)
E(explore) unknown, interval unknown: Gittins index



Notes
The situation: exploiting has a known expected outcome, E(exploit) = X. Exploring has an unknown outcome, E(explore) = ?. What should you do according to decision science?
Anecdotally: if you have a long interval, explore, choose B until you are sure about E(explore). If you have a short interval, exploit, choose A.
Takeaway: be sensitive to how much time you have left in the casino, and explore, explore, explore.

section: Explore gathers information, exploit uses it
text:
Explore gathers information, exploit uses it


🔍 Explore


Definition: Gathering new information
Risk: Unknown outcomes
Example: Trying that new sushi place



🎯 Exploit


Definition: Using known information
Risk: Missing better options
Example: Your go-to pizza joint










In any given moment you can only do one of the two.





The fundamental trade-off: explore and exploit are mutually exclusive choices in any given moment. You can’t have your cake and eat it too. Exploring means gathering new information with unknown outcomes, for example trying that new sushi place. Exploiting means using known information, with the risk of missing better options, for example your go-to pizza joint.

text:
A fair estimate: Laplace’s rule of succession

First we need a fair estimate of each machine
Laplace (18th century): after \(w\) wins and \(l\) losses, the chance of a win is about


\[\mathbb{E}[\text{win}] = \frac{w + 1}{w + l + 2}\]



In words: add one imagined win and one imagined loss, then take the share of wins


Pierre-Simon Laplace suggested this rule in the 18th century. The two added pulls keep the estimate away from 0 and 1 when we have seen very few pulls. The rule estimates how good a machine is; it does not tell us when to stop exploring.

section: Bellman: calculate backwards from the last pull
text:
Bellman: calculate backwards from the last pull

Richard Bellman found the exact solution for a known interval
Start at the final pull: with no future left, simply exploit
Then calculate backwards the best choice in every earlier situation


A few years after win-stay lose-shift, Richard Bellman found an exact solution for all cases with finite and known intervals. The question is when to stop exploring and start exploiting. The solution uses dynamic programming: start at the final pull and calculate backwards what the best choice is in every possible situation. This works because the last pull is easy.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Bellman needs to know how long you stay
text:
Bellman needs to know how long you stay

The calculation grows fast with many arms and a long interval
Worse: we usually don’t know how long we stay in the casino
So the bandit problem seemed to have no practical solution


The calculation of the optimal strategy is very extensive when there are many arms and a long interval. And the approach does not help in many scenarios, because we do not know the exact length of the interval. At this point it looked like the multi-armed bandit problem would remain a problem without a solution.

text:
Gittins: a drug-trial problem at Unilever1

1970s: Unilever asks the mathematician John Gittins to optimize its drug trials
Which compound is effective, found out as quickly as possible?
Gittins generalized the problem and found its optimal solution

For more details see Gittins, J. (1979) ‘Bandit Processes and Dynamic Allocation Indices’, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B (Methodological).

Earlier solutions needed a known interval
Gittins instead discounts future wins, like future cash flows
So any interval length works, even an endless one

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Gittins Index: The Scary Math
\[G_i(s_i, f_i) := \sup_{\tau \geq 1} \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \beta^t \cdot r_i^t \middle| s_i, f_i\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \beta^t\right]}\]
In words: the best average reward you can expect from this arm if you may stop playing it whenever you like.







Too complex to calculate by hand, and you don’t need to: just use the lookup table!

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Higher index, better choice

Core idea: “What’s the best possible average reward from this option?”
Higher index = better choice
Less-tested options get an exploration bonus, that’s why machine B wins
The index balances exploration and exploitation automatically

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Which rule when?

Both outcomes known: choose the higher expected value
E(explore) unknown, interval known: Bellman (backward calculation)
E(explore) unknown, interval unknown: Gittins index


The situation: exploiting has a known expected outcome, E(exploit) = X. Exploring has an unknown outcome, E(explore) = ?. What should you do according to decision science?
Anecdotally: if you have a long interval, explore, choose B until you are sure about E(explore). If you have a short interval, exploit, choose A.
Takeaway: be sensitive to how much time you have left in the casino, and explore, explore, explore.

EDD in real time: switch only for an earlier deadline

Always work on the task with the earliest deadline
A new task with an earlier deadline interrupts the current one
Otherwise, stick to the current task


Equal deadline: if a new task has the same deadline as the current task, you can choose either. But because of the cost of context switching, you should stick with the current task.

title: Tutorial I.II: Comparison Operators
text:
You’re teaching a computer to make decisions. Just like we compare things in everyday life (“Is it raining?”, “Do I have enough money?”), computers need ways to compare values and make choices. Let’s look at this in the context of hiring decisions to help us make decisions in the context of optimal stopping problems.
Imagine you’re helping a company make hiring decisions. You need to look at different candidates and decide if they meet certain requirements. To make these decisions with Python, we need to learn how to make comparisons!

Working with Lists
Lists are flexible. Here are the most common operations:

Adding items (like discovering a new restaurant):

append() adds to the end
insert() adds at a specific position



# Adding a new restaurant
restaurants = ["Pasta Place", "Sushi Bar"]
restaurants.append("Pizza Palace") # Adds to the end
print(restaurants)

# You can also insert at a specific position
restaurants.insert(1, "Taco Shop") # Adds at position 1
print(restaurants) # ["Pasta Place", "Taco Shop", "Sushi Bar", "Pizza Palace"]

['Pasta Place', 'Sushi Bar', 'Pizza Palace']
['Pasta Place', 'Taco Shop', 'Sushi Bar', 'Pizza Palace']



Removing items (like removing a restaurant you don’t like):

pop() removes the last item
remove() removes a specific item



# Removing the last restaurant
restaurants = ["Pasta Place", "Taco Shop", "Sushi Bar", "Pizza Palace"]
restaurants.pop() # Removes and returns the last item
print(restaurants)

# Removing a specific item
restaurants.remove("Pasta Place")
print(restaurants)

['Pasta Place', 'Taco Shop', 'Sushi Bar']
['Taco Shop', 'Sushi Bar']



Accessing items (like looking up a restaurant by position):

[0] gives you the first item
[1:3] gives you items second and third
[-1] gives you the last item



restaurants = ["Pasta Place", "Sushi Bar", "Burger Joint"]
first_choice = restaurants[0] # Gets "Pasta Place"
last_choice = restaurants[-1] # Gets "Burger Joint"
some_choices = restaurants[0:2] # Gets ["Pasta Place", "Sushi Bar"]







In Python, we start counting positions from 0, not 1. So restaurants[0] gives you the first restaurant!

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: What if you can be rejected?
text:
What if you can be rejected?
Question: In dating, the other person can also say no. Earlier or later than 37%?

50% chance of rejection: leap at 25%
Formula: \(q^{\frac{1}{1-q}}\), \(q\) = chance that your offer is accepted1
In words: the more often you hear “no”, the earlier you leap


Life lesson: higher risk of rejection means we should be less picky. With q = 0.5 the formula gives 0.5 to the power of 2, that is 25%. If offers are always accepted (q close to 1), the formula gives back the familiar 1/e.
Example from Brian Christian: searching from age 18 to 40, the 37% rule says get serious at 26.1. With many rejections, start at 23.5.

How it works: after the look phase, you ask everyone who beats all earlier candidates, and each says yes with chance \(q\). You get the best only if the best says yes and everyone you asked before said no. More rejections mean you use up more candidates after the look phase, so you have to start earlier. The stated formula is the best look phase, for example 25% when \(q = 50\%\). As in the basic problem, your chance of getting the best equals the look phase. With \(q\) close to 1, it gives back 37%.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: What if you can go back?
text:
What if you can go back?
Question: You can return to someone you passed on, but they might say no. Look longer or shorter?

Going back works only half the time: look at 61%1, then leap
If nobody better comes, return to the best you passed
In words: a second chance makes it safe to look longer


Example from the book: an immediate offer is always accepted, a belated one only with 50%. The safety net of going back shifts the look phase from 37% to 61%.

Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: What if you know how good an option is?
text:
What if you know how good an option is?
Question: Test scores, prices per square meter: do we still need a look phase?

Example: you know test scores, or the price per square meter of a flat
No look phase needed: take the first option above a threshold
The threshold drops as fewer options remain
Chance of getting the very best rises to 58%1


This is the “full information” version. With absolute scores and a known distribution, you don’t need to learn a benchmark first. The threshold starts high and falls as you run out of options.

Gilbert, J.P. & Mosteller, F. (1966). Recognizing the maximum of a sequence. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 61(313), 35–73.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
What if time is fixed?
Example: one year to find a flat, viewings come as they come

Question: How should we adapt our strategy?



Same principle: look for the first 37% of the time1, then leap
The number of options is not fixed: the harder we search, the more options we see


This holds if options arrive evenly over time. We can also decide how intensively we search, for example by viewing more flats per week. Searching harder in the look phase improves the benchmark.


Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The burglar: when to retire?
Example: each break-in succeeds with chance \(q\), one failure means losing everything

Question: Does the answer depend on \(q\), and how?



Stop after about \(\frac{q}{1-q}\) successes
With \(q = 90\%\): retire after 9 break-ins1
Same logic for any streak that can end badly: a winning run in the casino, a project that keeps growing in risk


Ferguson, T.S. Optimal Stopping and Applications. Lecture notes, University of California, Los Angeles, https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tom/Stopping/. The rule assumes the same haul every time: stop once your total haul is worth more than what you would expect to gain from one more attempt.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
What do people actually do?

In about a dozen experiments, people leap earlier than the 37% rule suggests1
Question: Why might that be?
Searching costs time and effort, and the rule ignores that
If looking is expensive, leaping earlier can be the right choice


Experiments by Seale and Rapoport (1997). The 37% rule assumes that looking is free. In real life, every viewing or interview costs time, so stopping a bit earlier is often rational, not a mistake.
Side note for drivers: an increase in occupancy from 90 to 95% doubles the search time for all drivers. Each variation changes the rule a little, but the structure stays: options come one at a time, and you cannot go back.

Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.
